description:
Five minds. One mission. Infinite possibilities beyond Earth.
Armed with code, AI, creativity, and a passion for building, we’re turning our academic ideas into experiences that bring space closer to Earth.
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we’re not just writing code—we’re designing, creating, and launching an idea of our own.
summary: VITAL is an offline health companion for astronauts on long missions. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline across five domains (immune, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, behavioral, metabolic) and raises early alerts, trend forecasts and suggested actions. It answers NASA's challenge by turning the hazards named by the Human Research Program (radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity fields, closed environments) into one monitoring tool. It pulls live NASA space-weather data (DONKI) and converts it into radiation guidance, and includes a mission planner built on NASA limits (600 mSv career dose, 250 mSv per solar storm). Because it runs onboard with no connection, it still works through a 22-minute Mars signal delay. It matters because crews far from Earth must make early health decisions on their own. Crew readings are simulated or entered by the user; reference values and space-weather feeds are real. Decision support, not diagnosis.
details:
Overview

VITAL (Crew Health Companion) is a health monitoring app for astronauts on long-duration missions. It gathers health indicators, compares each astronaut with their own baseline, and helps them judge and act on their health status without waiting for ground contact. It runs fully offline in a browser on a laptop or phone, and it pulls live NASA space-weather data when a connection exists.

Every screenshot below is from the real app. It is shown on a laptop screen and on a phone screen. Crew readings are simulated or entered by the user, because NASA does not publish astronauts' medical data. The reference values and space-weather feeds are real.

1. Summary

The Summary screen is the first thing an astronaut sees. A single 0 to 100 score shows overall health compared with that person's own baseline, with a plain label such as "Watch closely". A crew picker at the top shows every member with a colored status dot, so a commander can see the whole crew at a glance. Below it, a daily health mission lists the measurements still due today (blood pressure, blood oxygen, resting heart rate, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and fatigue) so routine checks are not forgotten.

2. Body map

The body map is a visual tool for self-assessment. The astronaut taps a body part (brain, lungs, heart, gut, muscles and bones, immune system) and the part is colored green, amber or red from their own data. The panel beside it shows the readings behind that status, why space affects that organ, which of NASA's five hazards is involved, what to do, and when to call the flight surgeon. The example shows the lungs: blood oxygen is normal, but respiration is amber, and the app explains that carbon dioxide can pool in microgravity. The environment picker (spacecraft in transit, space station, rover or surface traverse, Moon or Mars base) changes the risks and routine that are shown.

3. Trends

Each indicator has a 30-day chart with a shaded band showing that astronaut's normal range. A line leaving the band is an early warning, and a forecast shows when a metric may turn amber. Fifteen metrics are tracked, including heart rate, heart rate variability, sleep, skin temperature, mood, fatigue, pain, reaction time, stress, blood oxygen, blood pressure, respiration, blood glucose, exercise and radiation. Because the comparison is with the person's own history, a heart rate that is normal for one astronaut but unusual for another is still caught.

4. Hazards

This screen follows the five hazards of human spaceflight named by the NASA Human Research Program: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and hostile or closed environments. Each hazard shows the astronaut's own data, one action to take, and a link to the NASA source. The hazards are shown side by side because NASA notes they can feed off one another. For example, the distance card explains that a Mars reply takes about 44 minutes round trip, so the app gives answers onboard.

5. How to measure

Astronauts are not always medically trained, so every indicator has a guide that needs no medical background. Each guide covers how to take the measurement, why it matters in space, the normal range, and when to call the flight surgeon. Today's reading and status (green, amber or red) sit next to each guide, so the astronaut can check and log a value in one place. The guides cover blood pressure, resting heart rate, heart rate variability, blood oxygen, respiration rate, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and fatigue, and more.

6. Mission planner

The mission planner turns NASA limits into numbers for the crew. Sliders set mission length, radiation dose rate, shielding benefit and Earth to Mars one-way signal delay, and the app shows the radiation dose against NASA's 600 mSv career limit (with a 250 mSv per solar storm cap), estimated bone loss if exercise is skipped, and sleep debt. Presets such as "ISS, 6 months" and "Mars round trip" let a crew compare missions quickly.

7. Assistant (Nova)

Nova is an onboard assistant that reads the crew member's baseline and readings and answers in plain language. Quick questions include "Explain my status", "What should I focus on?", "Should I escalate?", "How is the crew?" and "Draft a note for the flight surgeon". The built-in assistant works offline with no key, which matters during a communications delay. Users can optionally connect their own Claude API key. The key stays in the browser. Answers always state that this is decision support, not diagnosis.

8. NASA data

This screen compares the astronaut's own numbers with NASA research values for sleep, radiation, exercise, reaction time, and mood and stress, with a status for each. It also shows the real NASA SpaceX Crew-13 mission on the International Space Station (names and mission are real; their health readings in the app are simulated). A separate Live NASA tab (not pictured) reads NASA DONKI solar flare, energetic particle and geomagnetic storm data and turns it into radiation guidance and a storm readiness score.

How it works

Each metric is compared with the person's own baseline spread. The score is z = (last 3 days minus first 7 days) divided by the baseline spread. A metric turns amber at z of 1 or more and red at z of 2 or more (adjustable). Metrics are grouped into five domains: immune, musculoskeletal, cardiovascular, behavioral and metabolic. Space-weather feeds are cached and fall back to the last good copy when offline.

Benefits and intended impact

Crews far from Earth must spot health changes in themselves and act early, with up to a 22-minute one-way delay to Mars. VITAL gives earlier detection of personal change, less reliance on delayed ground contact, and support for crew wellbeing. The same method also fits Antarctic stations, submarines and remote clinics.

Tools

HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript (no build step), inline SVG charts, a service worker and web manifest (installable, works offline), GitHub Pages for hosting, NASA DONKI and NASA Image and Video Library APIs, NOAA SWPC and wheretheiss.at feeds, and an optional Claude API connection using the user's own key. Parts of the code were written with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic) and reviewed by the team.

How it is creative

  • Personal baselines instead of population averages.
  • A storm readiness score that combines live space weather with the astronaut's own stressed domains.
  • A tappable body map tied to NASA's five hazards.
  • Live space weather turned into crew actions, not just data.
  • One app covering all five hazards, offline, on a laptop or a phone.

Factors we considered

  • Offline first: it works through a communication delay.
  • Privacy: data stays in the browser.
  • Accessibility: keyboard use, screen-reader labels, a skip link, high contrast and reduced motion.
  • Honest limits: readings are simulated, and thresholds need flight-surgeon validation before any real use.
  • Rules: no NASA logos, no images of anyone under 18, English only, and AI assistance disclosed.

Decision support, not diagnosis.
